lexemes.note: Literally “the first day”. On Sunday: בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן (no article). Written short: יוֹם א׳.

profile.feeling: Back to work: the first day of the Israeli week.

examples.tr: On Sunday I (m.) go back to work.

examples.text: בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן הוּא יוֹם עֲבוֹדָה.
examples.tr: In Israel Sunday is a working day.

synonyms.nuance: the written short form, with the letter א as the number 1 — on timetables, signs and in messages

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + רִאשׁוֹן “first”: the first day of the week counted from the Sabbath (Wiktionary lists the day names among the derived terms of יוֹם).

funFacts: Greek counts the same way from Sunday: Δευτέρα “second” is Monday, Τρίτη “third” Tuesday, Τετάρτη, Πέμπτη.
Arabic too: الْأَحَد “the one” is Sunday, الْإِثْنَيْن “the two” Monday.
pitfalls: In Israel the week starts on Sunday: יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן is a normal working day, not part of the weekend.
No article: בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן “on Sunday”. בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן is “on the first day”.
subtleties: Every weekday is a number: רִאשׁוֹן “first”, שֵׁנִי “second” … — only the seventh day has a name, שַׁבָּת.

lexemes.note: Literally “the second day”. On Monday: בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי (no article). Written short: יוֹם ב׳.

profile.feeling: The second working day; the week is under way.

examples.text: בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי יֵשׁ לִי שִׁעוּר עִבְרִית.
examples.tr: On Monday I have a Hebrew lesson.

synonyms.nuance: the written short form, with the letter ב as the number 2 — on timetables, signs and in messages

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + שֵׁנִי “second”: the second day of the week counted from the Sabbath (Wiktionary lists the day names among the derived terms of יוֹם).

funFacts: Greek Δευτέρα and Hebrew יוֹם שֵׁנִי both mean “second (day)”.
Arabic الْإِثْنَيْن “the two” is Monday — the same idea with a cardinal number.
pitfalls: שֵׁנִי is “second”, not “two” (שְׁנַיִם): Monday is “the second day”.
Chinese counts from Monday (星期一 “week-one” is Monday) — Hebrew counts from Sunday, so Monday is “two”.
subtleties: In speech the word יוֹם is often dropped: נִתְרָאֶה בְּשֵׁנִי “see you on Monday”.

lexemes.note: Literally “the third day”. On Tuesday: בְּיוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי (no article). Written short: יוֹם ג׳.

profile.feeling: A lucky day: a favourite day for weddings.

examples.tr: On Tuesday we are going to Jerusalem.

synonyms.nuance: the written short form, with the letter ג as the number 3 — on timetables, signs and in messages

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + שְׁלִישִׁי “third”: the third day of the week counted from the Sabbath (Wiktionary lists the day names among the derived terms of יוֹם).

funFacts: Greek Τρίτη, Arabic الثُّلَاثَاء and Hebrew שְׁלִישִׁי: Tuesday is “three” in all three.
pitfalls: Tuesday is the “third” day (שְׁלִישִׁי), not the “second”: count from Sunday.
subtleties: Many Jewish weddings are on Tuesday: on the third day of Creation “God saw that it was good” twice (Genesis 1:10 and 1:12).

lexemes.note: Literally “the fourth day”. On Wednesday: בְּיוֹם רְבִיעִי (no article). Written short: יוֹם ד׳.

profile.feeling: The middle of the working week.

examples.tr: Wednesday is the middle of the week.
On Wednesday he works from home.

synonyms.nuance: the written short form, with the letter ד as the number 4 — on timetables, signs and in messages

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + רְבִיעִי “fourth”: the fourth day of the week counted from the Sabbath (Wiktionary lists the day names among the derived terms of יוֹם).

funFacts: Greek Τετάρτη, Arabic الْأَرْبِعَاء (from أَرْبَعَة “four”) and Hebrew רְבִיעִי (from אַרְבַּע): Wednesday is “four” in all three.
pitfalls: The ע at the end of רְבִיעִי is pronounced in careful speech: revi‘i.
subtleties: German Mittwoch and Russian среда call it “the middle”; Hebrew just counts: “the fourth”.

lexemes.note: Literally “the fifth day”. On Thursday: בְּיוֹם חֲמִישִׁי (no article). Written short: יוֹם ה׳.

profile.feeling: The last working day: Thursday night is going-out night.

examples.tr: On Thursday evening we go out.
He is coming back from abroad on Thursday.

synonyms.nuance: the written short form, with the letter ה as the number 5 — on timetables, signs and in messages

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + חֲמִישִׁי “fifth”: the fifth day of the week counted from the Sabbath (Wiktionary lists the day names among the derived terms of יוֹם).

funFacts: Arabic الْخَمِيس “Thursday” has the same root as חֲמִישִׁי: “five” (خَمْسَة / חָמֵשׁ).
Greek Πέμπτη “fifth” is Thursday too.
pitfalls: Thursday is the fifth day: חֲמִישִׁי “fifth” (from חָמֵשׁ “five”).
subtleties: For most Israelis Thursday is the last working day, so Thursday evening is the big night out.

lexemes.note: Literally “the sixth day”. On Friday: בְּיוֹם שִׁשִּׁי (no article). Written short: יוֹם ו׳.

profile.feeling: A short day of shopping and cooking before Shabbat.

examples.text: בְּיוֹם שִׁשִּׁי אֲנַחְנוּ אוֹכְלִים אֵצֶל סָבְתָא.
examples.tr: On Friday we eat at Grandma’s.
On Friday the shops close early.

synonyms.nuance: the written short form, with the letter ו as the number 6 — on timetables, signs and in messages

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + שִׁשִּׁי “sixth”: the sixth day of the week counted from the Sabbath (Wiktionary lists the day names among the derived terms of יוֹם).

funFacts: Greek calls Friday Παρασκευή, “preparation” — for the Sabbath; Arabic الْجُمُعَة “the gathering” (the day of Friday prayer).
In Hebrew it is simply “the sixth (day)”, from שֵׁשׁ “six”.
pitfalls: Friday is part of the Israeli weekend: many offices are closed and shops close early, in the afternoon.
Friday evening is already Shabbat: עֶרֶב שַׁבָּת.
subtleties: Written in full spelling יום שישי; the vowelled form has a dagesh in the second ש: שִׁשִּׁי.

lexemes.note: Saturday — the only weekday with a name. בְּשַׁבָּת “on Saturday / on Shabbat”; שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם is the greeting from Friday afternoon on.

profile.feeling: Quiet streets, family meals, no buses: the day of rest.

senses.def: the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest

examples.tr: On Saturday we are at home.
On Shabbat there are no buses in most cities.

phrases.meaning: the Sabbath greeting (from Friday afternoon on)

phrases.tr: remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy

synonyms.nuance: the full name, “the Sabbath day” (Wiktionary lists it among the day names)

etymology.text: Possibly borrowed from Akkadian šapattum (“the middle day of the lunar month”) (Wiktionary). The verb שָׁבַת “to stop working, rest” has the same letters.

funFacts: Greek Σάββατο, Russian суббота and German Samstag go back to this word; Arabic السَّبْت “Saturday” is its Semitic cousin.
A sabbatical year (שְׁנַת שַׁבָּתוֹן) is a “Sabbath” of a year — from the same word.
pitfalls: Feminine: שַׁבָּת שְׁקֵטָה “a quiet Shabbat”.
Saturday is שַׁבָּת — there is no *יוֹם שְׁבִיעִי in use.
subtleties: Shabbat starts on Friday at sunset and ends on Saturday night: the Jewish day runs from evening to evening.
מוֹצָאֵי שַׁבָּת “the going-out of Shabbat” is Saturday night — a lively evening in Israeli towns.

lexemes.note: The weekend — in Israel Friday and Saturday. “At the weekend” = בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ (the article goes on the second word). Colloquial short form סוֹפָ״שׁ.

profile.feeling: Friday and Saturday: the beach, the family, a trip up north.

senses.def: the end of the week (בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ “at the end of this week”)

examples.tr: What are you (m.) doing at the weekend?
The report will be ready at the end of the week.

collocations.tr: at the weekend; at the end of the week

synonyms.nuance: the short form, from the first letters: “sofash” (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: סוֹף “end” + שָׁבוּעַ “week”; Wiktionary gives no etymology and lists the short form סוֹפָ״שׁ.

funFacts: The short form סוֹפָ״שׁ is written with gershayim, like other Hebrew abbreviations (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The Israeli weekend is Friday and Saturday — Sunday is a working day.
With the article only the second word changes: סוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ; plural סוֹפֵי שָׁבוּעַ.
subtleties: בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ can mean “at the weekend” or “at the end of the week” — the context decides.

lexemes.note: Irregular plural יָמִים. “Two days” is the dual יוֹמַיִם. With the article, הַיּוֹם is also the word “today”.

profile.feeling: Every day, all day, a good day.

senses.def: a time, era (בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם “in those days”)

examples.tr: There are seven days in a week.
Every day I (m.) go to work.

phrases.text: וַיְהִי עֶרֶב וַיְהִי בֹקֶר יוֹם אֶחָד
phrases.tr: and there was evening and there was morning, one day

phrases.meaning: day and night, all the time

synonyms.nuance: “a full day of 24 hours” — technical: פַּעַם בִּיְמָמָה “once every 24 hours”

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *yawm-, with *aw becoming ō; cognate with Arabic يَوْم (yawm) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic يَوْم (yawm) is the same word (Wiktionary).
The days of the week are all “day + number”: יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן, יוֹם שֵׁנִי …
pitfalls: The plural is irregular: יָמִים (not *יוֹמִים).
הַיּוֹם is both “the day” and “today” — almost always “today”.
Two days is normally the dual יוֹמַיִם (rather than שְׁנֵי יָמִים).
subtleties: The Jewish day begins in the evening: “there was evening and there was morning — one day” (Genesis 1:5); Wiktionary gives the sense “from a nightfall until the following nightfall”.

lexemes.note: Masculine although it ends in -ָה: לַיְלָה טוֹב. Plural לֵילוֹת. “At night” = בַּלַּיְלָה; “tonight” = הַלַּיְלָה.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ / לָ (בְּ / לְ + the article), which drop the ה of the article: הַלַּיְלָה → (בַּ / לַ)לַּיְלָה; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַלַּיְלָה.

profile.feeling: Dark, quiet, the stars over the desert.

examples.tr: At night the children are asleep.
Tonight we are staying at home.

phrases.meaning: day and night, all the time

synonyms.nuance: the poetic and older form (Wiktionary lists it as a synonym)

etymology.text: Likely a remnant of the accusative (adverbial “at night”) of לַיִל, from Proto-Semitic *layl-; cognate with Arabic لَيْل (layl), لَيْلَة (layla) and Aramaic לֵילְיָא (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Thousand and One Nights are אֶלֶף לַיְלָה וְלַיְלָה in Hebrew.
Arabic لَيْلَة (layla) — and the name Layla — are the same word (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Masculine despite the -ָה: לַיְלָה אָרֹךְ “a long night”, לַיְלָה טוֹב “good night”.
Plural לֵילוֹת — masculine, but with -וֹת.
subtleties: הַלַּיְלָה with the article is “tonight”, like הַיּוֹם “today”, הַבֹּקֶר “this morning”.
The final ה is not a feminine ending: it is probably an old case ending (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: “In the morning” = בַּבֹּקֶר; “this morning” = הַבֹּקֶר. Full spelling בוקר.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ / לָ (בְּ / לְ + the article), which drop the ה of the article: הַבֹּקֶר → (בַּ / לַ)בֹּקֶר; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַבֹּקֶר.

profile.feeling: Coffee, the first bus, “good morning”.

examples.tr: In the morning I (f.) drink coffee.
Every morning she runs in the park.

phrases.meaning: said to someone who has only just noticed what everyone knows

synonyms.nuance: “dawn, daybreak” — the very first light

etymology.text: From the root ב־ק־ר, which appears only in pi‘el: בִּקֵּר “inspected” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Breakfast is אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר, “the morning meal” (lesson 7).
The answer to בֹּקֶר טוֹב can be בֹּקֶר אוֹר, “morning of light” (lesson 2).
pitfalls: “In the morning” needs the article: בַּבֹּקֶר (not *בְּבֹקֶר).
Masculine: בֹּקֶר טוֹב “good morning”, בֹּקֶר יָפֶה.
subtleties: הַבֹּקֶר is “this morning” — the article alone means “this”, as in הַיּוֹם, הָעֶרֶב, הַלַּיְלָה.

lexemes.note: A dual form, masculine, no plural: noon and the early afternoon (about 12–3). “At noon” = בַּצָּהֳרַיִם. Full spelling צהריים.

profile.feeling: Midday heat, lunch, a short nap.

senses.def: noon, midday (the middle of the day, about 12–3)

examples.tr: At noon we eat at home.

examples.text: הוּא מַגִּיעַ בְּשָׁעָה שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה בַּצָּהֳרַיִם.

synonyms.nuance: “midday” — exactly twelve o’clock

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic ظُهْر (ẓuhr) and Aramaic ṭahrā; a dual, like עַרְבַּיִם “dusk” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic ظُهْر is the same word: صَلَاةُ الظُّهْرِ is the noon prayer (Wiktionary gives the cognate).
pitfalls: Masculine and dual-looking (-ַיִם), but one noon: no plural.
בַּצָּהֳרַיִם is a stretch of time (about 12–3), not only twelve o’clock.
subtleties: שְׁנַת צָהֳרַיִם “a noon sleep” is a nap, written short שנ״צ (Wiktionary).
The first vowel is a short o (tsohoráyim), as in אֲרוּחַת צָהֳרַיִם.

lexemes.note: “In the afternoon”, without a preposition: אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם אֲנִי בַּבַּיִת. Written short אחה״צ.

profile.feeling: After lunch: homework, the park, coffee.

examples.tr: In the afternoon I am at home.
The children are in the park in the afternoon.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday pronunciation, with אַחֲרֵי “after”
the written abbreviation, on timetables and in messages

etymology.text: אַחַר “after” + הַצָּהֳרַיִם “the noon” (the parts are in Wiktionary; the phrase has no entry of its own).

funFacts: English “afternoon”, German Nachmittag and Hebrew אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם are all built the same way: “after-noon”.
pitfalls: No בְּ in front: אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם “in the afternoon” — unlike בַּבֹּקֶר, בָּעֶרֶב.
subtleties: “This afternoon” is הַיּוֹם אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם.

lexemes.note: “In the evening” = בָּעֶרֶב; “this evening” = הָעֶרֶב. Before a holiday: עֶרֶב שַׁבָּת “Shabbat eve (Friday evening)”.

profile.feeling: Sunset, dinner, a walk when it gets cooler.

senses.def: eve, the day before (a holiday): עֶרֶב שַׁבָּת, עֶרֶב פֶּסַח

examples.tr: In the evening we eat dinner.
This evening I (m.) am staying at home.
On Shabbat eve the whole family is at home.

synonyms.nuance: “towards evening”, late afternoon (Wiktionary)
“at dusk, twilight” (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Cognates include Arabic غَرْب (ḡarb, “west”) (Wiktionary) — the west is where the sun sets in the evening.

funFacts: Arabic غَرْب “west” is the same Semitic word (Wiktionary) — and so is the name Maghreb (الْمَغْرِب), “the place of sunset”.
pitfalls: “In the evening” takes the article: בָּעֶרֶב (בְּ + הָ); “this evening” is הָעֶרֶב alone.
עֶרֶב + a holiday is the day before: עֶרֶב שַׁבָּת is Friday (evening), not Saturday evening.
subtleties: The Jewish day begins in the evening — so עֶרֶב comes first in “there was evening and there was morning” (Genesis 1:5).

profile.feeling: Here and now: today’s plans.

synonyms.nuance: “nowadays, at present” — in writing

etymology.text: הַ “the” + יוֹם “day” (Wiktionary): “the day” = today.

funFacts: German heute comes from a phrase meaning “on this day” — Hebrew says just “the day”.
pitfalls: Today is “the day”: הַיּוֹם looks exactly like הַיּוֹם “the day” (יוֹם with the article) — almost always it means “today”.
subtleties: The same pattern gives הַבֹּקֶר “this morning”, הָעֶרֶב “this evening” and הַלַּיְלָה “tonight”.

profile.feeling: Plans and promises: see you tomorrow.

examples.tr: Tomorrow I (m.) am going to Haifa.

phrases.tr: eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

synonyms.nuance: “the next day” — in a story about the past or the future, not “tomorrow from today”

etymology.text: Probably a prefixed formation related to אַחַר “hind part, after”; cognate with Aramaic מחר (Wiktionary).

funFacts: מָחָר is related to אַחַר “after” (Wiktionary): tomorrow is “the after-day”.
pitfalls: With מָחָר the present tense is enough for a plan: מָחָר אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ “tomorrow I’m going” — as in German Morgen fahre ich.
“The next day” in a story is לְמָחֳרָת, not מָחָר.
subtleties: The day after tomorrow is a dual: מָחֳרָתַיִם (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: Speaking about yesterday needs the past tense (lesson C01); for now: אֶתְמוֹל הָיָה יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן “yesterday was Sunday”.

profile.feeling: What happened: yesterday’s news.

phrases.meaning: I’m not naive, you can’t fool me

synonyms.nuance: the older, literary form (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: A form with a prefixed vowel of the now literary תְּמוֹל; compare Aramaic אֶתְמָלִי and Akkadian ittimali (timāli with a prefix) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Aramaic אֶתְמָלִי and Akkadian ittimali add the same kind of prefix to the old word for “yesterday” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: It needs a past-tense verb or הָיָה “was”: אֶתְמוֹל הָיָה יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן.
The day before yesterday is שִׁלְשׁוֹם, not *לִפְנֵי אֶתְמוֹל.
subtleties: תְּמוֹל שִׁלְשׁוֹם “yesterday and the day before” is a literary “formerly”.

lexemes.note: Written without vowels as עכשיו (with a י).

profile.feeling: Right now, this minute.

synonyms.nuance: “now, at present” — the news, official texts
“now” — Biblical and poetic

etymology.text: Perhaps from עַד כְּשָׁעָה or עַד כְּשֶׁהוּא; attested since Late Antiquity. The spelling with י keeps the reader from reading the ו as “o” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same trick of spelling — a silent י before the final ו — is in סתיו “autumn” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Unvowelled it is written עכשיו — the י is silent: akhshav.
subtleties: עַד עַכְשָׁו “until now” also means “so far”: עַד עַכְשָׁו הַכֹּל בְּסֵדֶר.

profile.feeling: First this, then that.

senses.def: then, after that (the next step in a sequence)

examples.tr: First we eat, then we go out.

examples.text: הוּא קוֹנֶה לֶחֶם, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הוּא חוֹזֵר הַבַּיְתָה.
examples.tr: He buys bread, and then he goes back home.

synonyms.nuance: “after that”
“thereafter” — written style
“later” in the sense of “at a later time” (lesson 17: comparatives)
“and then” — the usual link in a story (lesson 18)

etymology.text: From אַחַר “after” + כָּךְ “so, thus” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: German danach / nachher and Hebrew אַחַר כָּךְ are built alike: “after” + “that / so”.
pitfalls: Two words, with a final ךְ: אַחַר כָּךְ.
אַחַר כָּךְ stands alone (“afterwards”); before a noun use אַחֲרֵי: אַחֲרֵי הָאֲרוּחָה (lesson 15).
subtleties: קֹדֶם … אַחַר כָּךְ “first … then” is the usual way to put steps in order.

profile.feeling: Coming soon: “see you soon!”.

synonyms.nuance: “in a little while” — sooner, in the next minutes
“right away, in a moment”

etymology.text: From בְּ “in” + קָרוֹב “close, near” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Literally “in near”: time is spoken of as distance, as in English “in the near future”.
pitfalls: Not “near”: קָרוֹב is “near” (lesson 12); בְּקָרוֹב is “soon”.
subtleties: עוֹד מְעַט and תֵּכֶף are minutes away; בְּקָרוֹב can be days or weeks.

lexemes.note: Full spelling מוקדם. Also an adjective (“early, preliminary”).

profile.feeling: The first bus, an early start.

synonyms.nuance: “early in the morning, at daybreak”

etymology.text: From the root ק־ד־ם “before, in front” (as in קֹדֶם “first, before” and קָדִימָה “forward”); Wiktionary gives no etymology of its own.

funFacts: The same root gives קֶדֶם “the east” — where the day begins.
pitfalls: Full spelling מוקדם; do not confuse unvowelled מקדם with מְקַדֵּם “promotes; coefficient”.
subtleties: As an adjective it agrees: בְּחִירוֹת מֻקְדָּמוֹת “early elections”.

lexemes.note: Full spelling מאוחר. To be late (for something) is the verb אִחֵר: הוּא מְאַחֵר “he is late”.

override.meaning: Wiktionary files מְאֻחָר “late, belated” only as an adjective (a page reached through its defective spelling); the only adverb under the same letters is מֵאַחַר “since, because”, another word. מְאֻחָר is the everyday adverb “late” (הוּא חוֹזֵר מְאֻחָר).

profile.feeling: The last bus, a late dinner.

examples.tr: He comes back late from work.

phrases.meaning: it is better to do something late than not at all

synonyms.nuance: “with a delay” — a train or a flight that is late

etymology.text: The past participle of אִחֵר “to be late” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: מְאֻחָר and אַחַר “after” share the root א־ח־ר: being late is being “after”.
pitfalls: “He is late” (not on time) is the verb: הוּא מְאַחֵר — not *הוּא מְאֻחָר.
Full spelling מאוחר.
subtleties: מְאֻחָר מִדַּי “too late” (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Habits that never change.

examples.tr: I (m.) always drink tea in the evening.
As always, the bus is late.

synonyms.nuance: “all the time” — often with a complaint
“ever, forever”; with a negation “never”

etymology.text: Of uncertain origin: Ernest Klein connects it with מוד, related to מדד “to measure” and Arabic مَدَّ “to stretch”; others think of עמד “to stand” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The daily Temple offering was called הַתָּמִיד, “the constant (one)”.
pitfalls: Usually before the verb: הוּא תָּמִיד בָּא (after the verb is possible, but less common).
subtleties: לְתָמִיד “forever” and נֵר תָּמִיד “the eternal light” of a synagogue (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: Full spelling לעיתים קרובות. In speech people often just say הַרְבֵּה “a lot”.

profile.feeling: Things that happen again and again.

synonyms.nuance: “a lot”: אֲנַחְנוּ נוֹסְעִים הַרְבֵּה לְחֵיפָה
“frequently” — written style

etymology.text: From לְעִתִּים “at times” and קָרוֹב “close, near” (Wiktionary): “at close times”.

funFacts: Time as distance again: “often” is “at near times”, “rarely” “at far times”.
pitfalls: It sounds a little formal; in conversation הַרְבֵּה is more natural.
Full spelling לעיתים קרובות.
subtleties: The opposite is לְעִתִּים רְחוֹקוֹת “rarely”, literally “at far-apart times” (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Now and then.

synonyms.nuance: “from time to time”
“at times”

etymology.text: From לְ “to, for” + פְּעָמִים “times” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Built like German manchmal and Greek μερικές φορές: “(some) times”.
pitfalls: פְּעָמִים alone is “times” (שָׁלוֹשׁ פְּעָמִים “three times”); with לְ it becomes “sometimes”.
subtleties: After לְ the פּ softens: lif‘amim.
